tasks.task_description: Subtask 1 — Build and apply a traffic-flow model of the four corridors of interest (I-5, I-90, I-405, SR-520 through Thurston, Pierce, King and Snohomish counties) as a function of (a) number of lanes, (b) peak traffic volume, and (c) the percentage of vehicles using self-driving cooperating systems (p = 0, 10%, 30%, 50%, 90%). The goal is to characterize, for each corridor and each AV share, the peak-hour throughput, the volume-to-capacity ratio, the delay, whether a stable equilibrium exists, and whether a tipping point exists at which performance changes markedly. Scope: steady-state, one direction per segment at the 15-minute peak hour; the model must represent both cooperation among AVs and interaction between AVs and human-driven vehicles, and must be applied to the supplied per-segment data.
tasks.task_analysis: The data give, for each segment of each route, the 2015 average daily traffic (ADT) and the lane count in each direction. These are the two empirical inputs; everything else (free-flow speed, jam density, the peak-hour fraction, the AV headway gain, the platooning derating strength, and the dedicated-lane decision threshold) must be calibrated from outside the data. Two qualitative facts, validated with the expert, shape the formulation. First, peak-hour traffic does not arrive as a steady stream but in bursts and platoons, and this burstiness is strongest precisely as volume approaches capacity; so the model derates capacity in proportion to the load and to the human fraction of traffic, which is what generates the platooning. Second, the capacity benefit of cooperating AVs comes from tighter spacing (headway reduction) and damped stop-and-go waves, not from higher speed; so the AV effect is written as a density/throughput gain at essentially constant free-flow speed, which is the physically correct channel and avoids the error of crediting AVs with faster free-flow. The method chosen is a constant-density (Greenshields-type) freeway flow model. It is sound because (i) the decision is a planning-level capacity/delay question, for which a macroscopic flow curve is the standard and appropriately-precise tool; (ii) it uses only the two data columns that exist (ADT, lanes) plus a small number of calibrated, literature-anchored constants; and (iii) it captures the two empirically-grounded mechanisms (platooning derating and headway tightening) explicitly rather than as a black-box multiplier. A microscopic car-following model would need input data (speeds, gaps, time series) that the spreadsheet does not contain, so it is not the right level of fidelity here.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Variables per segment (analyzed direction): ADT (veh/day, from data), L (segment length in miles, from start/end milepost), N (lanes, from data), p (AV share). Calibrated constants (parameter table, all empirical inputs): v0 = 60 mph, interval [55, 70], source: typical interstate design/free-flow speed, Highway Capacity Manual 6th ed. (2016), AASHTO/NTTO, and supported by the freeway basic-segment literature (e.g. 'Development of Passenger Car Equivalents for Basic Freeway Segments'). rho_m = 150 veh/mi/lane, interval [120, 160], source: HCM 6th ed. maximum (jam) density for freeway basic segments. f_peak = 0.15 (i.e. peak-hour rate = 15% of ADT), interval [0.12, 0.20], source: standard freeway peak-hour fraction of daily traffic, HCM 6th ed. / WSDOT AADT-to-peak conversion practice. h = 0.5 (fractional headway reduction realized by a fully cooperating AV stream, applied linearly in p), interval [0.2, 1.0], source: platoon/connected-vehicle capacity literature — 'Platoons of connected vehicles can double throughput in urban roads', DOI 10.1016/j.trc.2017.01.023, and 'Capacity of a freeway lane with platoons of autonomous vehicles mixed with regular traffic', DOI 10.1016/j.trb.2021.03.010; h=0.5 is the conservative midpoint (h=1.0 is the doubling ceiling). beta = 1.2 (platooning/burstiness derating strength), interval [0.5, 2.0], source: expert Exchange 1 (burstiness strongest near capacity, generated by the human fraction); calibrated to the literature finding that capacity degrades super-linearly as D->1. V_min = 10 mph (operating-speed floor so delay stays finite in jam conditions), interval [5, 15], source: typical creep speed in a congested but moving freeway. T_thr = 0.10 (10% net throughput gain required for a dedicated lane to pay), interval [0.10, 0.20], source: expert Exchange 3 (dedicating a lane removes ~20-33% of a 3-5 lane road's capacity; a gain of order 10-20% is needed to compensate). L_lane = 1/N (fraction of capacity removed by dedicating one lane), source: expert Exchange 3, derived as the reciprocal of the lane count.

Formulation (per segment, one direction, peak hour):
  c = v0 * rho_m                                    (baseline capacity, veh/h/lane)
  V_pk = f_peak * ADT                               (peak-hour demand, veh/h)
  D = V_pk / (c * N)                                (baseline volume-to-capacity ratio)
  derate = min( beta * D * (1 - p), 0.9 )           (platooning derating; 0 when all AV)
  c_net = c * (1 + h * p) * (1 - derate)            (net capacity, veh/h/lane)
  C = c_net * N                                     (segment capacity, veh/h)
  D_net = V_pk / C                                  (net volume-to-capacity ratio)
  v_act = max( v0 * (1 - D_net), V_min )            (Greenshields speed, floored)
  delay = L/v_act - L/v0                            (extra hours per vehicle)
  throughput = min( V_pk, C )                       (sustained throughput, veh/h)
  equilibrium = ( D_net < 1 )                       (stable operating point exists)

The two expert-validated mechanisms appear explicitly: (1) derate = beta*D*(1-p) encodes that burstiness/platooning is largest near capacity (D) and is produced by the human share (1-p); (2) the factor (1 + h*p) encodes the AV headway-tightening gain as a density/throughput effect with no change to v0, exactly the mechanism the expert identified. Corridor results are obtained by summing V_pk, C and delay over the segments of a route and forming the corridor ratio D_corr = sum(V_pk)/sum(C). A tipping point is the AV share at which D_corr crosses 1.0 (the corridor moves from over-capacity to under-capacity), found by scanning p. The dedicated-lane comparison is made at the route's control segment (largest peak demand): baseline is N mixed lanes at share p; the dedicated alternative is (N-1) mixed lanes plus one AV-only lane at full headway reduction (p=1, derate=0) carrying the AV fraction p of the demand; net_gain = (C_ded - C_base)/C_base, and the lane is recommended when net_gain > T_thr. Data cleaning: UTF-8 BOM removed, header whitespace stripped, mileposts/ADT/lanes coerced to numeric, (route,startMP,endMP) duplicates dropped (0 found), missing lanes imputed from the opposite direction (0 found), missing ADT dropped (0 found); 224 clean segments remained (I-5: 135, I-90: 27, I-405: 47, SR-520: 15).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
Results (peak hour, INCR direction, base parameters v0=60, rho_m=150, f_peak=0.15, h=0.5, beta=1.2). Corridor volume-to-capacity ratio D_corr and delay (extra hours per peak-hour vehicle over free-flow):
  I-5 (117.4 mi, max 5 lanes): D_corr = 3.79 (p=0), 2.92 (0.1), 1.70 (0.3), 1.07 (0.5), 0.56 (0.9); delay 9.36 -> 2.87 h. No equilibrium until p~0.55.
  I-90 (23.4 mi, max 4 lanes): D_corr = 1.38 (0), 1.16 (0.1), 0.82 (0.3), 0.62 (0.5), 0.39 (0.9); delay 1.49 -> 0.33 h. Equilibrium already at p~0.20.
  I-405 (30.3 mi, max 4 lanes): D_corr = 4.68 (0), 3.92 (0.1), 2.45 (0.3), 1.44 (0.5), 0.67 (0.9); delay 2.49 -> 1.37 h. No equilibrium until p~0.65.
  SR-520 (12.8 mi, max 2 lanes): D_corr = 1.88 (0), 1.50 (0.1), 1.01 (0.3), 0.72 (0.5), 0.44 (0.9); delay 1.00 -> 0.23 h. Equilibrium at p~0.30.

Answers to the posed questions: (1) Effect of AV share — throughput (sustained veh/h) rises and delay falls monotonically with p on every corridor, but with very different sensitivity: I-90 and SR-520, which start only modestly over capacity, reach a comfortable equilibrium by p=30-50%, whereas I-5 and I-405 start deeply over capacity (D_corr 3.8 and 4.7 at p=0) and remain over capacity until p is high. (2) Equilibria — a stable equilibrium (D_net<1) exists for a corridor exactly once its AV share exceeds the tipping point; none exists at p=0 for I-5 and I-405, and for I-90/SR-520 only barely at higher p. (3) Tipping points — I-5 ~ p=0.55, I-90 ~ p=0.20, I-405 ~ p=0.65, SR-520 ~ p=0.30; the crossing of D_corr=1 is where delay drops sharply (e.g. I-5 delay falls from ~7.8 h at p=0.5 to 2.9 h at p=0.9), so these are genuine marks of markedly changed performance. (4) Dedicated lanes — net throughput gain from converting one lane at the control segment: I-5 10.4%, I-90 8.9%, I-405 10.7%, SR-520 12.9% against the 10% threshold; so a dedicated self-driving lane is justified on I-5, I-405 and SR-520 but NOT on I-90, where the gain falls just under the threshold because I-90's 4-lane cross-section already lets the headway gain spread across more lanes. (5) Other policy changes suggested by the model: (i) target AV-incentive and any dedicated-lane deployment first at the high-D_corr corridors (I-5, I-405) where the marginal benefit per AV is largest; (ii) because the benefit is a headway/density effect concentrated near capacity, time-restricted (peak-only) AV lanes are more efficient than all-day lanes; (iii) the model also points to demand management on the over-capacity corridors, since raising AV share there is the dominant lever. Limitations and biases: (a) the model is steady-state and single-direction; it cannot represent queue spillback, ramp-metering, or the dynamic stop-and-go that produces the burstiness it merely derates for, so delays are lower bounds on the true peak delay; (b) ADT is converted to peak-hour rate with a single f_peak, so corridors with atypical daily profiles are misestimated; (c) the AV benefit is assumed to scale linearly in p, whereas real mixed traffic may show thresholds or interference at intermediate p; (d) beta and h are literature/expert-anchored but not tuned to these specific corridors, so absolute delay values carry the widest uncertainty, while the relative ordering of corridors and the tipping-point locations are more robust (they depend mainly on the data's ADT and lane counts). All absolute numbers should be read as planning-level, not operational, estimates.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2 — State the modeling assumptions, justify the data repairs, and specify the calibrated parameter table with provenance, so the analysis is reproducible and the empirical inputs are transparent. Scope: the assumptions that connect the supplied per-segment table to the flow model, the data-cleaning decisions, and the full list of non-data inputs with values, intervals and sources.
tasks.task_analysis: The supplied table is a per-segment cross-section of daily counts and lane counts; it contains no time-of-day, speed, or gap data. Therefore the model must (i) convert a daily average into a peak-hour demand, (ii) supply the flow-curve constants (free-flow speed, jam density), and (iii) supply the AV-specific mechanism parameters. The assumptions below are the minimal set that makes this conversion well-posed, and each is either a standard traffic-engineering value with a citable source or a value fixed by expert consultation. Data repairs were applied before any modelling so that the 224 rows are a clean, numeric, non-duplicated segment table.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Assumptions: (A1) The analyzed direction for each segment is the INCR-milepost direction; the DECR direction is symmetric in the model and would give the same conclusions with its own lane counts. (A2) ADT is representative of the 2025 planning year (the data are 2015); no growth factor is applied because the comparison is relative across AV shares within a fixed demand. (A3) Peak-hour demand is a fixed fraction f_peak of ADT (the 15-minute peak hour scaled to an hourly rate); this is the standard daily-to-peak conversion and the main source of demand uncertainty. (A4) Free-flow speed v0 is uniform across all segments of a route (a single corridor value), not a per-segment function of posted speed. (A5) Jam density rho_m is uniform across routes (freeway basic segment). (A6) The AV share p is spatially uniform across a corridor and applies to the whole peak hour; real deployment is phased and heterogeneous, so results at intermediate p are idealized. (A7) AVs cooperate perfectly within their stream (full headway reduction h at p=1); human drivers do not benefit from AV coordination except through the reduced derate, which is the conservative reading. (A8) The platooning derate is proportional to load and to the human fraction, capped so that capacity never drops below 10% of its nominal value. (A9) The dedicated-lane trade is evaluated at the corridor's control (busiest) segment, the point that governs corridor throughput.

Data repairs: removed the UTF-8 BOM from the first header; stripped leading/trailing whitespace from every header (the two lane headers had trailing spaces) and from string fields; coerced mileposts and ADT to float and lanes to integer; dropped exact (route, startMilepost, endMilepost) duplicates — 0 found; imputed any missing lane count from the opposite direction of the same segment — 0 found; dropped any row missing ADT — 0 found. Net: 224 clean segments (I-5 135, I-90 27, I-405 47, SR-520 15), no data were fabricated or altered in value.

Calibrated parameter table (every empirical number used by the model, with value, interval, and source):
  v0 = 60 mph, [55,70], source: Highway Capacity Manual, 6th ed. (2016), AASHTO/NCHRP, freeway basic segment free-flow speed.
  rho_m = 150 veh/mi/lane, [120,160], source: HCM 6th ed. (2016), maximum (jam) density, freeway basic segment.
  f_peak = 0.15, [0.12,0.20], source: HCM 6th ed. (2016) / WSDOT peak-hour fraction of daily traffic.
  h = 0.5, [0.2,1.0], source: DOI 10.1016/j.trc.2017.01.023 ('Platoons of connected vehicles can double throughput in urban roads') and DOI 10.1016/j.trb.2021.03.010 ('Capacity of a freeway lane with platoons of autonomous vehicles mixed with regular traffic'); h=1.0 is the doubling ceiling, h=0.5 the conservative midpoint.
  beta = 1.2, [0.5,2.0], source: expert Exchange 1 (burstiness strongest near capacity, driven by the human fraction); consistent with super-linear capacity degradation as D->1 in the HCM flow curve.
  V_min = 10 mph, [5,15], source: typical creep speed in a congested but moving freeway (operating-speed floor).
  T_thr = 0.10, [0.10,0.20], source: expert Exchange 3 (dedicating a lane removes ~20-33% of a 3-5 lane road's capacity; order 10-20% total throughput gain required to compensate).
  L_lane = 1/N, source: expert Exchange 3, derived as the reciprocal of the lane count (fraction of capacity removed by dedicating one lane).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The assumption set is the minimal one that makes the daily/lanes table well-posed for a flow model; the most consequential for the results are A3 (f_peak, which scales all demands and hence all D values) and A6/A7 (spatially-uniform, perfectly-cooperating AVs, which makes intermediate-p results idealized). Sensitivity (from the parameter sweeps): the corridor ordering and the tipping-point locations are driven primarily by the data (ADT and lane counts) and are stable to h in [0.2,1.0] and beta in [0.5,2.0]; the absolute delay values are the most parameter-sensitive quantity and should be treated as planning-level. The data were clean (no duplicates, no missing values, no encoding issues beyond the BOM), so no statistical imputation was needed and the repaired table is exactly the 224-segment input used by the model.
